title: The talking mind
hook: brain areas busy during mind-wandering were quieter in experienced meditators in a 2011 study (Brewer et al.)

segments.voice: Yesterday: six breaths a minute. Your line was six a minute. Did you find a red light or a checkout line to try it in? Day three hundred nine.

You're brushing your teeth. Nobody is talking to you. And yet there's talking. Should have said that differently in the meeting. What's for dinner. Why did she text like that. Remember to buy batteries. It's a radio you never switched on, playing in the next room, mostly about you. Most of us assume that's just what a mind is. Scientists got curious about it too, and in 2011 a team at Yale put experienced meditators into a brain scanner to see what happens to that radio when people practice. This week is about habits, kindness and each other. It starts with the voice in your head. Today: the talking mind.
screen: `BRUSHING YOUR TEETH.` → `A RADIO IN THE NEXT ROOM.` → `MOSTLY ABOUT YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the brain. Around the turn of this century, researchers noticed that when people lie in a scanner doing nothing in particular, certain brain areas get busier, not quieter. They called this network the default mode network: what the brain does by default. It's busy when we daydream, replay the past, plan, and think about ourselves. Then the 2011 study. Judson Brewer and colleagues scanned a small group of experienced meditators and a group of beginners. During meditation, key parts of that default network were less active in the experienced group. Small study, one snapshot, remember compared to what. It doesn't prove meditation rewires anyone. But it fits what meditators have described for centuries. Second, the stream. William James, the American psychologist, wrote in 1890 that our thinking is not a row of separate bricks. In his words, "It is nothing jointed; it flows." A stream, he said, is the natural picture. You don't turn a stream off. You can sit on the bank. Third, the old noticing. Many meditation teachers, especially in Buddhist insight practice, teach a simple move: when a thought grabs you, name it softly. Thinking. Planning. Worrying. The naming makes a small gap between you and the voice. You are the one hearing it, which means you're not only the voice. That brings us to why it matters on a Tuesday. The talking mind isn't an enemy. It plans dinners and solves problems. But much of its chatter is rehearsal and replay, and a lot of it is harsher than you would ever be to a friend. You can't unplug the radio. You can notice it's on, and turn it down a notch.
screen: `THE DEFAULT MODE NETWORK.` · `QUIETER IN EXPERIENCED MEDITATORS.` · `IT IS NOTHING JOINTED; IT FLOWS.` · `NAME IT: THINKING, PLANNING.` · then, large: `THE TALKING MIND.`

segments.voice: For the next two minutes, just listen to your own inner talk, like overhearing a stranger on a bus. When a sentence shows up, give it a quiet label. Planning. Remembering. Judging. Then come back to one breath. Don't argue with what it says, and don't try to make it stop. Notice the tone, too. Is it kind? Hurried? Bossy? You're only listening. The bell holds the time.
The talking mind. The stream of inner chatter, much of it about ourselves, tied in the lab to the brain's default mode network. Today's word.
Your line: the talking mind. Three times today, catch the voice mid-sentence and name what it's doing: planning, replaying, judging. Just the name. Day three hundred nine.

screen: `DAY 309 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW LONG A HABIT TAKES.`

howItsDone: Many meditation teachers, especially in Buddhist insight practice, teach noting: when a thought arises, the meditator names it softly, such as thinking or planning, and returns to the breath.

myth: the brain goes quiet when you're doing nothing
some areas, the default mode network, get busier when we're idle.
the 2011 study proves meditation rewires the brain
it was a small snapshot study; it fits the picture, but proves no such thing.
William James compared thought to a stream
in 1890 he wrote that thinking flows, and isn't jointed like bricks.

fork.setup: you sit to practice, and the voice in your head starts replaying an argument. what do many meditation teachers suggest?
options: name it softly, then return to the breath.
stop meditating: you're doing it wrong.
fork.reveal: noting: call it replaying or thinking, and come back. the thought showing up isn't failure; noticing it is the practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: the talking mind is a problem to shut off.
what it means: the inner stream of chatter, useful and noisy, that you can learn to notice.
what a scholar hears: the default mode network, named by Marcus Raichle's lab in 2001, and Brewer's 2011 finding of less activity there in experienced meditators.

notes: Brewer et al. 2011: about a dozen experienced meditators vs a similar number of novices; main nodes of the DMN (medial prefrontal and posterior cingulate cortex) relatively deactivated in meditators. Confirm group sizes are 'small' and summary is fair.
Default mode network: Raichle et al. 2001 coined 'default mode'; confirm.
James quotation, Principles of Psychology (1890), vol. 1, ch. IX 'The Stream of Thought': confirm exact wording.
Noting practice attributed generally to Buddhist insight (vipassana) teachers; the script doesn't name a lineage.
